Beat 1 — invite (attach Fig 1 overview)

Your coding agent keeps using the same outside loop for an easy shell job and a nasty repo fix.

Score stalls even when the model is locked. Walk with me through a paper that rebuilds that loop per task.

203 chars

Beat 2 — harness + Fan dock

That outside loop is the harness: which tools the model may call, what checks run, what state is kept, when to stop.

Fan’s harness-design work already showed this layer can decide whether a run even survives. Today is about how you assemble it.

245 chars

Beat 3 — two bad defaults

Two common defaults both hurt.

One fixed harness forever (Mini-SWE-agent style) and every task shares wiring never chosen for it. Generate a whole new harness from scratch per task and the paper’s own model says the chance it stays runnable falls as pieces stack.

264 chars

Beat 4 — STITCH mechanism (Fig 1 if not on #1)

STITCH (Selects suitable primitives given Task Information, then compiles them into a Task-specific Harness) does the third thing.

It mines failed runs for small, already-tested harness pieces, each with a clear when-to-use scope. At test time a picker matches pieces to this task. A fixed compiler wires them into something that actually runs. No new harness code written per task.

383 chars (over 280)

Beat 5 — RRSI contrast (cold-reader gloss)

RRSI (Recursive Reflective Self-Improvement) is a different dock in the same neighborhood: it rewrites the whole scaffolding in a recursive loop under guardrails so it does not just memorize train tasks.

STITCH keeps a library of validated pieces and composes at test time. Same idea that the harness matters. Different verb: evolve-all vs pick-and-wire.

355 chars (over 280)

Beat 6 — TB2 punch + MetaHarness (Table 2)

On Terminal-Bench 2 (shell and environment tasks; 45 sampled, two attempts each), same GPT-5.6-Luna held frozen on purpose:

Mini-SWE-agent seed: 60.0% Pass@1 (share solved on a single try). STITCH: 72.2%. +12.2 percentage points.

MetaHarness is the harness-optimization baseline here: it searches for a better whole loop. STITCH instead picks already-validated pieces and wires them. Same model. Same tasks. Only how the outside loop was assembled changed.

458 chars (over 280)

Beat 7 — SWE punch (same table)

Same pattern on Software Engineering Benchmark Verified (SWE-bench Verified, N=100):

Seed 73.0% → STITCH 80.5% (+7.5 percentage points). Pass squared (both attempts succeed): 68.0% → 76.0%.

190 chars

Beat 8 — cost (Fig 4)

Building that per-task harness costs 2.7% of one actor attempt on Terminal-Bench.

At least 638× cheaper than a lower-bound generate-from-scratch path.

151 chars

Beat 9 — library scales (Fig 2)

Pass@1 rises as the primitive library grows. More validated pieces on the shelf, better picker matches.

103 chars

Beat 10 — uncertainty close

What I still want measured is how often the picker grabs a piece that fixed yesterday’s failure mode and hurts today’s, and whether you can catch that before the compiled loop ships.

If you run agents across mixed jobs, that is the question worth instrumenting.

262 chars

Beat 11 — takeaway + link

A global harness still leaves points on the table when the instrument picker misfires — or when you never pick at all.
